newsitem.title: UK: Dollar to find limited ammunition if US hikes rates.
newsitem.headline: Dollar to find limited ammunition if US hikes rates.

text.p: Foreign exchange dealers believe the United States will raise interest rates on Tuesday by 0.25 percent but only a 0.5 percent increase would seriously affect the dollar.

The market was pricing in a 25-basis points rise at Tuesday's rate-setting meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Markets Committee and only a surprise 50-point increase will shake it out of its recent levels, analysts said.

"After all the speculation regarding the outcome of this meeting a 25 basis points tightening of the Fed funds rate would come as something of an anti-climax," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.
Such a move would ward off traders who are bearish aboput the dollar, while inaction might prompt losses in some of the recent dollar gains.
Mark weakness rather than independent strength has prompted the dollar's recent revival to two-month highs, analysts said.

A new wave of enthusiasm about European economic and monetary union (EMU) has pushed the mark down, and the display of enthusiasm for EMU at the European finance ministers' meeting in Dublin last weekend triggered further mark sales.
At 1120 GMT the dollar traded at 1.5167 marks and 109.83 yen compared with 1.5144 and 109.80 in late European trading on Friday.
If Tuesday's meeting failed to sanction a rise, the dollar would be at risk of weakening as some of the long positions built up in the run-up to the meeting would be wound down, traders said.

Inaction would fuel suspicion that political forces are influencing monetary policy ahead of the elections in November. In addition, hawkish forces in the market, worried about inflation, would take fright.

"If the FOMC keeps rates unchanged it's likely to be a dollar-negative as those concerned about inflation might consider the Fed to be behind the game," said David Bloom, currency economist at HSBC James Capel.
A larger than expected rise could give the dollar upside momentum initially but some also argue that it might backfire since the market might consider it as a panic move.

"A bigger than expected move would increase the market's worry about inflation, and a negative response in the asset markets would likely spill over into the dollar," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International.

A poll conducted by Reuters last week showed that opinion remains divided. A slim majority of economists polled -- 17 of 30 -- believed the Fed would opt to raise short-term rates, with all but one of those analysts expecting a small increase of one-quarter percentage point.
Analysts expect this week's FOMC gathering to be one of its more contentious, as members contemplate raising interest rates for the first time in about a year and a half.

Anti-inflation hawks, principally at the Fed's regional banks, argue for a rise to keep inflation at bay. The doves, mostly political appointees on the Fed board in Washington, question whether rates should rise when the economy is slowing.
The economy, in the words of Fed Governor Janet Yellen, is operating in an "inflationary danger zone". But so far there is no sign of a pick-up in inflation.
At 5.1 percent, the unemployment rate is at its lowest in more than seven years and at a level that in the past has usually led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation.
Wages, in fact, have already begun to pick up but so far U.S. companies have been unable to pass on those higher labour costs to consumers in the form of price increases.

The FOMC last sanctioned an interest rate change in January, when it cut the Federal funds and the discount rate both by a quarter point. The Fed funds rate now stands at 5.25 percent and the discount rate at 5.00 percent.
